entries.content_osis: <div eID="gen34338" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen34339" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen34340" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen34340" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen34339" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen34341" type="x-p"/> This chapter opens with a tender and pathetic lamentation, in the style of a funeral song, over the house of Israel, <reference osisRef="Amo.5.1">Amo 5:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Amo.5.2">Amo 5:2</reference>. The prophet then glances at the awful threatening denounced against them, <reference osisRef="Amo.5.3">Amo 5:3</reference>; earnestly exhorting them to renounce their idols, and seek Jehovah, of whom he gives a very magnificent description, <reference osisRef="Amo.5.4-Amo.5.9">Amo 5:4-9</reference>. He then reproves their injustice and oppression with great warmth and indignation; exhorts them again to repentance; and enforces his exhortation with the most awful threatenings, delivered with great majesty and authority, and in images full of beauty and grandeur, <reference osisRef="Amo.5.10-Amo.5.24">Amo 5:10-24</reference>. The chapter concludes with observing that their idolatry was of long standing, that they increased the national guilt, by adding to the sins of their fathers; and that their punishment, therefore, should be great in proportion, <reference osisRef="Amo.5.25-Amo.5.27">Amo 5:25-27</reference>. Formerly numbers of them were brought captive to Damascus, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.10.32">2Kgs 10:32</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.10.33">2Kgs 10:33</reference>; but now they must go beyond it to Assyria, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.29">2Kgs 15:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.6">2Kgs 17:6</reference>. <div eID="gen34341" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34342" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen34342" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34343" type="x-p"/> Hear ye this word - Attend to this doleful song which I make for the house of Israel.
entries.content_plain: Introduction This chapter opens with a tender and pathetic lamentation, in the style of a funeral song, over the house of Israel, Amo 5:1 , Amo 5:2 . The prophet then glances at the awful threatening denounced against them, Amo 5:3 ; earnestly exhorting them to renounce their idols, and seek Jehovah, of whom he gives a very magnificent description, Amo 5:4-9 . He then reproves their injustice and oppression with great warmth and indignation; exhorts them again to repentance; and enforces his exhortation with the most awful threatenings, delivered with great majesty and authority, and in images full of beauty and grandeur, Amo 5:10-24 . The chapter concludes with observing that their idolatry was of long standing, that they increased the national guilt, by adding to the sins of their fathers; and that their punishment, therefore, should be great in proportion, Amo 5:25-27 . Formerly numbers of them were brought captive to Damascus, 2Kgs 10:32 , 2Kgs 10:33 ; but now they must go beyond it to Assyria, 2Kgs 15:29 ; 2Kgs 17:6 . Verse 1 Hear ye this word - Attend to this doleful song which I make for the house of Israel.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen34344" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34345" type="x-p"/> The city that went out by a thousand - The city that could easily have furnished, on any emergency, a thousand fighting men, can now produce scarcely one hundred - one in ten of the former number; and now of the hundred scarcely ten remain: so reduced was Israel when Shalmaneser besieged and took Samaria, and carried the residue into captivity.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen34346" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34347" type="x-p"/> But seek not Beth-el - There was one of Jeroboam's golden calves, and at Gilgal were carved images; both were places in which idolatry was triumphant. The prophet shows them that all hope from those quarters is utterly vain; for Gilgal shall go into captivity, and Beth-el be brought to naught. There is a play or paronomasia on the letters and words in this clause: הגלגל גלה יגלה ובית אל יהיה לאון haggilgal galoh yigleh, ubeith el yiheyeh leaven. "This Gilgal shall go captive into captivity; and Beth-el (the house of God) shall be for Beth-aven," (the house of iniquity.)

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen34370" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34371" type="x-p"/> Wo unto you that desire the day of the Lord - The prophet had often denounced the coming of God's day, that is, of a time of judgment; and the unbelievers had said, "Let his day come, that we may see it." Now the prophet tells them that that day would be to them darkness - calamity, and not light - not prosperity.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen34371" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34372" type="x-p"/> As if a man did flee from a lion, and a bear met him - They shall go from one evil to another. He who escapes from the lion's mouth shall fall into the bear's paws: - <div eID="gen34372" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34373" type="x-p"/> Incidit in Scyllam, cupiens vitare Charybdim. <div eID="gen34373" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34374" type="x-p"/> The Israelites, under their king Menahem, wishing to avoid a civil war, called in Pul, king of Assyria, to help them. This led to a series of evils inflicted by the Syrian and Assyrian kings, till at last Israel was ravaged by Shalmaneser, and carried into captivity. Thus, in avoiding one evil they fell into another still more grievous. <div eID="gen34374" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34375" type="x-p"/> Leaned his hands on a wall, and a serpent bit him - Snakes and venomous animals are fond of taking up their lodging in walls of houses, where they can either find or make holes; and it is dangerous to sit near them or lean against them. In the East Indies they keep the faithful mongose, a species of ichneumon, in their houses, for the purpose of destroying the snakes that infest them.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen34375" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34376" type="x-p"/> I hate, I despise your feast days - I abominate those sacrificial festivals where there is no piety, and I despise them because they pretend to be what they are not. This may refer to the three annual festivals which were still observed in a certain way among the Israelites.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen34377" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34378" type="x-p"/> The noise of thy songs - the melody of thy viols - They had both vocal and instrumental music in those sacrificial festivals; and God hated the noise of the one and shut his ears against the melody of the other. In the first there was nothing but noise, because their hearts were not right with God; and in the latter there could be nothing but (זמרת zimrath) cutting and scraping, because there was no heart - no religious sense in the thing, and nearly as little in them that used it. See on <reference osisRef="Amo.6.5">Amo 6:5</reference> (note).

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen34379" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34380" type="x-p"/> Have ye offered unto me sacrifices - Some have been led to think that "during the forty years which the Israelites spent in the wilderness, between Egypt and the promised land, they did not offer any sacrifices, as in their circumstances it was impossible; they offered none because they had none." But such people must have forgotten that when the covenant was made at Sinai, there were burnt-offerings and peace-offerings of oxen sacrificed to the Lord, <reference osisRef="Exo.24.5">Exo 24:5</reference>; and at the setting up of the tabernacle the twelve princes of the twelve tribes offered each a young bullock, a ram, and a lamb, for a burnt-offering; a kid for a sin-offering; two oxen, five rams, five he-goats, and five lambs, for a peace-offering, <reference osisRef="Num.7.12">Num 7:12</reference>, etc.; which amounted to an immense number of victims offered in the course of the twelve days during which this feast of the dedication lasted. At the consecration of priests, bullocks and rams to a considerable number were offered, see <reference osisRef="Lev.8.1">Lev 8:1</reference>, etc.; but they were not offered so regularly, nor in such abundance, as they were after the settlement in the promised land. Learned men, therefore, have considered this verse as speaking thus: Did ye offer to me, during forty years in the wilderness, sacrifices in such a way as was pleasing to me? Ye did not; for your hearts were divided, and ye were generally in a spirit of insurrection or murmuring.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen34380" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34381" type="x-p"/> But ye have borne - The preceding verse spoke of their fathers; the present verse speaks of the Israelites then existing, who were so grievously addicted to idolatry, that they not only worshipped at stated public places the idols set up by public authority, but they carried their gods about with them everywhere. <div eID="gen34381" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34382" type="x-p"/> The tabernacle of your Moloch - Probably a small portable shrine, with an image of their god in it, such as Moloch; and the star or representative of their god Chiun. For an ample exposition of this verse, see the note on <reference osisRef="Act.7.42">Act 7:42</reference>; to which let me add, that from Picart's Religious Ceremonies, vol. 3 p. 199, we find that there was an idol named Choun worshipped among the Peruvians from the remotest antiquity.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen34382" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34383" type="x-p"/> Will I cause you to go into captivity beyond Damascus - That is, into Assyria, the way to which, from Judea, was by Damascus. <div eID="gen34383" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34384" type="x-p"/> But St. Stephen says, <reference osisRef="Act.7.43">Act 7:43</reference>, beyond Babylon; because the Holy Spirit that was in him chose to extend the meaning of the original text to that great and final captivity of the Jews in general, when Zedekiah, their last king, and the people of Judea, were carried into Mesopotamia, Armenia, and Media; see <reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.7">2Kgs 17:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.24">2Kgs 17:24</reference>. This captivity happened after the time of Amos.  <chapter eID="Amos.5"/> <div eID="gen34384" type="x-p"/>

navigation_sections.title: Introduction
navigation_sections.content_plain: Introduction This chapter opens with a tender and pathetic lamentation, in the style of a funeral song, over the house of Israel, Amo 5:1 , Amo 5:2 . The prophet then glances at the awful threatening denounced against them, Amo 5:3 ; earnestly exhorting them to renounce their idols, and seek Jehovah, of whom he gives a very magnificent description, Amo 5:4-9 . He then reproves their injustice and oppression with great warmth and indignation; exhorts them again to repentance; and enforces his exhortation with the most awful threatenings, delivered with great majesty and authority, and in images full of beauty and grandeur, Amo 5:10-24 . The chapter concludes with observing that their idolatry was of long standing, that they increased the national guilt, by adding to the sins of their fathers; and that their punishment, therefore, should be great in proportion, Amo 5:25-27 . Formerly numbers of them were brought captive to Damascus, 2Kgs 10:32 , 2Kgs 10:33 ; but now they must go beyond it to Assyria, 2Kgs 15:29 ; 2Kgs 17:6 .
